Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models
as Single-Pass Decision Makers

Ziyi Chen Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Yan Zhang Affiliation: National University of Singapore    Jianhui Wei Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Jianing Yin Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania    Daoan Zhang Affiliation: University of Rochester
Abstract

Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182×\times speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning’s accuracy advantage while generating 27–58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.

Keywords: 
Large Decision Models, schema transfer, distillation, evaluation

1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 2National University of Singapore
3Zhejiang University 4University of Pennsylvania 5University of Rochester

1 Introduction

Many applications require a decision: route a support ticket, judge whether a claim is supported, or rate an incident’s severity. Large Language Models (LLMs) acquire broad knowledge through pretraining and generalize across diverse tasks. However, generating decisions through autoregressive decoding (rollout) incurs latency and computational costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities, limiting their suitability for tasks that require fast responses and confidence-aware choices. Conventional BERT-based classifiers offer efficient predictions, but task-specific fine-tuning ties their output heads to predefined labels (Devlin et al., 2019). To combine classification efficiency with the generality of pretrained language models, we study Large Decision Models (LDMs), which map a context, a question and a label set specified at run time to a distribution over the labels in a single forward pass—an operation we call readout (§2; Fig. 1). Existing systems such as Jev, Nimble, OpenJev and Laya offer this interface (TypeSafe, 2026; Bespoke Labs, 2026; OpenJev authors, 2026; Convai Innovations, 2026).

To adapt LLM rollout to LDM readout, we use decision tuning: given a context, a question and candidate labels, we fine-tune the model with LoRA to predict the correct label by applying cross-entropy to the normalized option-token logits at the final input position, without generating any sequence. After training, we evaluate schema transfer: accuracy on decision schemas, label sets and domains absent from fine-tuning, alongside calibration and single-pass cost. Schema transfer is feasible because pretraining already places most of the decision in the representation that a single forward pass reads. Without any decision training, the readout of an untuned 27B model reaches 97% of its tuned accuracy, and 1/16 of the tuning data recovers 88% of the tuning gain at 9B (§4). Decision tuning is therefore an adaptation of how that representation is read out, not the acquisition of new task knowledge.

Our diagnosis identifies two opportunities for improving transfer (§4). First, decision tuning improves source accuracy more reliably than new-schema accuracy, motivating supervision across broader schemas. Second, reasoning rollout reveals capabilities that the single-pass readout does not fully express: on two new-schema validation sets, the same untuned 27B model is 7.8–9.3 points more accurate when allowed to reason. This rollout–readout gap motivates two complementary uses of reasoning: distillation during training and selective computation at inference.

Our training recipe builds on these two opportunities (§5). Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS) uses synthetic decision schemas to promote generalization beyond familiar tasks and output patterns. Varying domains, rules and label meanings, alongside public and instruction data, encourages the readout to interpret each new schema. Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) aims to bring readout performance closer to that of the base model using reasoning rollout. It distils a reasoning teacher’s answer distributions on new self-posed tasks into the readout, making those decisions a training target while retaining single-pass inference.

At deployment, a confidence router combines fast readout with selective reasoning rollout. It accepts confident readout answers and sends uncertain decisions to the base model for reasoning rollout, using a threshold fixed on validation data (§5.3).

We evaluate DDS and SPRD separately and together across three base models from two families, with three seeds each (§6). We introduce DecisionVista, a benchmark suite pairing new decision schemas (DecisionVista-Synth) with human-labelled tasks from eight sources excluded from fine-tuning and method design (DecisionVista-Human). Our protocol separates model development from pre-registered testing on these two sets (§3). Averaged across bases, the combined recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 points on DecisionVista-Synth and 1.5 on DecisionVista-Human. Against a baseline selected on validation data, it gains 0.8 points on DecisionVista-Human and 2.1 on the public typed-decisions benchmark. Our 9B model outperforms Nimble-9B on the same base across transfer evaluations and Nimble-13. On Gemma-4-31B served on two H100 GPUs, tuned readout reduces median latency from 7.38 s to 40.6 ms, a 182×\times speedup over reasoning rollout (Table 4). On validation sets, routing recovers a median 92% of the rollout–readout gap using 27–58% of full reasoning’s generated tokens (§6).

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    LDM formulation: single-pass decision models centered on generalization to unseen schemas.

  2. 2.

    DDS and SPRD: a training recipe combining synthetic schema diversity with distillation of a reasoning teacher’s decisions.

  3. 3.

    DecisionVista: synthetic and human-labelled benchmarks, with a protocol separating model development from pre-registered testing.

  4. 4.

    Confidence routing: a deployment strategy combining fast readout with selective reasoning rollout.

  5. 5.

    Statistically validated gains: our recipe improves accuracy over the step-matched baseline by 1.8 points on DecisionVista-Synth (95% CI [0.6, 3.1]) and 1.5 on DecisionVista-Human (95% CI [0.9, 2.2]). Tuned readout achieves a 182×\times median-latency speedup over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B.

2 Large Decision Models

A Large Decision Model (LDM) maps a context cc and a decision schema specified at run time to a probability distribution over the schema’s allowed outcomes in a single forward pass. A schema consists of a question or decision rule qq and a finite label set 𝒴\mathcal{Y} with natural-language descriptions:

pθ(⋅∣c,q,𝒴)∈Δ(𝒴),p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c,q,\mathcal{Y})\in\Delta(\mathcal{Y}), (1)

where Δ⁡(𝒴)\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) is the set of probability distributions over 𝒴\mathcal{Y}; the predicted outcome is arg⁡maxy∈𝒴​pθ​(y∣c,q,𝒴)\arg\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{\theta}(y\mid c,q,\mathcal{Y}). Schemas may express categorical choices, binary judgements or ordinal ratings, with label meanings and any ordering supplied at run time. This allows the same model to address new decisions without a task-specific output head or further training.

A pretrained model can use this interface zero-shot. Decision tuning aligns the model with this interface by adapting autoregressive rollout to single-pass readout. Jev (TypeSafe, 2026) serves this interface as a hosted service; Nimble-9B (Bespoke Labs, 2026) and OpenJev-27B (OpenJev authors, 2026) release LLM weights for it, and Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026) a 0.3–0.4B encoder with a trained decision head. An LDM should be judged first on schema transfer, accuracy on decision schemas, label sets and domains absent from fine-tuning, and then on calibration and cost.

3 Evaluating schema transfer

Testing schema transfer requires both comparison with existing systems and evidence that gains extend beyond the tasks used to develop the recipe. We therefore separate public comparisons, model selection and exploratory diagnosis from independent confirmation (Table 1).

Public benchmarks and development sets.

Public benchmarks anchor comparisons with released decision models: Nimble’s full 13-subset benchmark (Nimble-13) (Bespoke Labs, 2026) and the typed-decisions test set reported for Jev and Laya (Typed-Decisions) (Convai Innovations, 2026); four workflows, labels from an LLM teacher. Typed-decisions contains 2,000 decisions across 400 cases (five per case); its authors report 73.5% repeatability of the teacher labels. No model in the primary study trains on their sources. Table 3 also reports Kev’s transfer-v4 test (Kev-Transfer; 656 items from sources new to Kev, including MMLU and QNLI), read once.

The human-labelled validation suite (Val.) supports model selection, temperature calibration and routing thresholds. Other validation sets probe complementary forms of transfer: the human-labelled transfer suite tests generalization across sources, while synthetic DV-Dev-A/B test newly constructed decision schemas. These sets guide recipe development, so gains on them require confirmation on untouched sets. The human-suite sources are excluded from fine-tuning, and synthetic evaluation families are screened against training schemas. DV-Dev-A/B contain rule-based decisions written in contrastive groups by gpt-5.5 and kept when gpt-6-astra agreed blind. Source inventories and the earlier DV-Stress and DV-Pilot stages are in Appendices N and D.

DecisionVista tests.

The two primary sets were constructed after the primary models were frozen, then sealed and first read under pre-registered analyses; no design decision used them. DecisionVista-Synth tests newly constructed schemas: 35 families over 18 decision operators, including capacity allocation, Pareto choice and counterfactual intervention. Four model families author the tasks; the three non-authors label each item blind, and at least two must agree with the author (Appendix K). Families are screened against earlier evaluation families and training schemas; we claim screened non-overlap, not freedom from pretraining exposure. Its labels are model agreement, not human judgement; a human audit protocol is released. We also evaluate without the author that verified synthetic DDS labels (Appendix M). DecisionVista-Human complements this test with 2,299 human-labelled items from eight sources absent from all training mixtures, earlier evaluation sets and Super-NaturalInstructions tasks (Appendix L). Here the held-out units are sources; related task types can appear in training. Tables abbreviate the pair to DV-Synth and DV-Human.

Measurement and protocol.

The primary statistics are mean accuracy across task families on DecisionVista-Synth and across sources on DecisionVista-Human, averaged equally across bases. Paired bootstrap intervals resample task families or items within each human-labelled source; a two-level sensitivity analysis also resamples training seeds (Appendix C). Nimble scores average its 13 subset accuracies; typed-decisions intervals resample its 400 cases. Calibration uses negative log-likelihood (NLL), Brier score and expected calibration error (ECE; 15 bins). Appendix D records which sets informed each choice; analyses specified after the sealed reads are marked post hoc. Pre-registrations, hashes, per-item predictions and code are in the supplementary material.

4 Diagnosing schema transfer

Our exploratory diagnosis asks why decision tuning transfers unevenly and how much accuracy the single-pass readout leaves unused. Two observations motivate broader schema supervision and reasoning-derived targets.

The decision is largely already in the representation.

Across Qwen3.5 sizes from 0.8B to 27B, the untuned single-pass readout reaches 76–97% of the accuracy of the same model after decision tuning, the tuning gain shrinks from 15.8 to 2.3 points as the base grows, and 1/16 of the tuning data already recovers most of it (Appendix T). Pretraining thus supplies the representation; tuning adapts how it is read. The adaptation is light but must reach the backbone: LoRA updates under 0.5% of the parameters, whereas training only the option-letter head on frozen features recovers almost none of the gain (Appendix U).

Source gains do not ensure schema transfer.

We rebuilt Nimble’s recipe and varied scale, data, objective and capacity (Appendix B). At 27B, training on 20k records from 36 public datasets raises validation accuracy from 79.3 to 81.8; adding the public benchmark’s training sources gives 89.1 on its eight choice and yes/no subsets, versus OpenJev’s 84.1. Yet neither recipe consistently improves new-schema accuracy: the public-data recipe scores 88.1/87.5 on DV-Dev-A/B and the source-augmented recipe 87.8/88.0, against the untuned model’s 89.1/87.5. Transfer depends on scale and evaluation set—baseline tuning does help at 9B—so this is a motivation to broaden schema coverage, not a claim that supervised tuning cannot transfer.

The rollout–readout gap.

The same untuned 27B model is more accurate when allowed to reason (majority of four samples): 96.9 vs. 89.1 on DV-Dev-A, 96.8 vs. 87.5 on DV-Dev-B and 85.1 vs. 79.3 on the validation suite (Table 7). Where the two modes disagree on DV-Dev-B, reasoning is right 90% of the time. A separate single-sample analysis finds the largest gains on exact multi-step computation (dates and numeric comparisons: 56–66% readout, 98–100% reasoning across the three bases), while reasoning can lose on NLI (Appendix P). Reasoning costs hundreds of generated tokens per decision. These observations motivate DDS to broaden the schemas encountered during training and SPRD to train the readout toward a reasoning teacher’s decisions, paying for teacher computation offline. Confidence routing retains access to reasoning for uncertain decisions at deployment.

5 Training LDMs for schema transfer

We train the readout to interpret unfamiliar decision schemas and to approximate decisions available from a reasoning teacher. DDS broadens schema coverage through synthetic decisions alongside public and instruction data; SPRD supplies reasoning-derived answer distributions on self-posed tasks. At deployment, a confidence router can send uncertain decisions to the student’s untuned base using reasoning rollout.

Implementation.

For this study, we implement the LDM interface by normalising the logits of single-token option identifiers:

pθ​(y∣c,q,𝒴)=softmaxy∈𝒴zθ​(ℓy∣x⁡(c,q,𝒴)),p_{\theta}(y\mid c,q,\mathcal{Y})=\operatorname*{softmax}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\,z_{\theta}\big(\ell_{y}\mid x(c,q,\mathcal{Y})\big), (2)

where x⁡(⋅)x(\cdot) serialises the context, question and options, ℓy\ell_{y} is the letter assigned to outcome yy, and zθ​(ℓy∣x)z_{\theta}(\ell_{y}\mid x) is its logit at the final input position. We support choice (2–8 named options), yes/no, and ordinal score (3–6 ordered levels); these bounds are implementation choices, not part of the LDM definition. Each instruction-tuned base trains a LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022) on this readout, with option order re-shuffled at every draw. The baseline training data contain 22.4k public and contrastive records (Appendix H).

5.1 Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS)

Learning a common answer format does not by itself ensure that the readout can apply unfamiliar decision rules. DDS uses synthetic task construction to vary domains, rules and label meanings, aiming to encourage schema interpretation beyond the original training tasks. Public datasets and categorical instruction tasks (Wang et al., 2022) provide complementary coverage, while the readout objective stays fixed.

Each run uses the same 31.7k-record sample from the 63.4k pool: additional public sources, Super-NaturalInstructions tasks, and synthetic decisions built from a domain–decision grid or grounded in real documents (Appendix J). Synthetic labels require blind verification, and synthetic schemas are audited against evaluation families. The pool excludes benchmark-source data and is 13-gram de-contaminated against evaluation items available at construction; the later DecisionVista sets are checked against the frozen mixtures (Appendices K, L).

5.2 Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD)

SPRD turns the rollout–readout gap into supervision: the readout learns decisions reached with additional computation, without learning to generate the reasoning trace. Qwen3.8-27B is the frozen task author and reasoning teacher for all primary students; only the 27B student learns from its own untuned base.

Self-posed tasks and decision targets.

The teacher proposes schemas across domains, reasoning skills and answer formats, then writes contrastive instances for schemas that pass an evaluation-family audit: 16,040 items from 696 schemas (Appendix N). It answers each item four times using reasoning rollout. The target is q⁡(y∣x)=ny/mq(y\mid x)=n_{y}/m, where nyn_{y} counts votes for yy and mm is the number of parseable samples. Requiring the top vote share over all four samples to be at least 0.75 retains 14,829 items. The consistency-filtered variant, SPRD-C, further keeps the 10,331 items whose reasoning majority agrees with the label intended at item construction. This checks consistency between two computations of the same model, not correctness. The student receives answer distributions, never reasoning traces.

Joint training.

Baseline data and DDS records supply supervised labels; pool records supply teacher distributions. We shuffle the enabled data streams together and minimise their mean per-record loss:

ℓθ​(r)={−log⁡pθ​(yr⋆∣xr),r∈𝒟sup,λDKL(qr∥pθ(⋅∣xr)),r∈𝒟S​P​R​D,\ell_{\theta}(r)=\begin{cases}-\log p_{\theta}(y^{\star}_{r}\mid x_{r}),&r\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{sup}},\\[2.0pt] \lambda\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_{r}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{r})\big),&r\in\mathcal{D}_{SPRD{}},\end{cases} (3)

where 𝒟sup\mathcal{D}_{\text{sup}} contains baseline data plus DDS when enabled, and λ=3\lambda=3. Inference remains one forward pass.

5.3 Confidence routing to reasoning

The router accepts confident readout decisions and sends uncertain items to that student’s untuned base using reasoning rollout (one sample). Its score is the top-two margin m⁡(x)=log⁡pθ​(y(1)∣x)−log⁡pθ​(y(2)∣x)m(x)=\log p_{\theta}(y_{(1)}\mid x)-\log p_{\theta}(y_{(2)}\mid x), equal to the corresponding logit gap in Eq. 2. If m⁡(x)<τm(x)<\tau, the reasoning answer is used; otherwise the readout’s answer stands at zero generated tokens. We fix τ\tau at the bb-quantile of margins on the validation suite, with b=30%b=30\% unless stated, before reading other sets. This sets validation coverage; the fraction routed on an unseen set can differ. The router requires no additional training.

6 Results

We first test transfer on the pre-registered evaluations, then examine component effects, compare released models and evaluate confidence routing. We compare baseline training alone, with DDS, with SPRD-C, and with both on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, using the fixed Qwen teacher from §5.2. The primary comparator, step-matched baseline, trains for 4,032 steps against the full recipe’s 4,031 at batch size 16 (2.9 passes over baseline data). We report three seeds per variant; the pre-registered test estimates use seeds 17/29/41 at 9B and 17/29 at 27B/31B, excluding later seed-41 runs (Appendix H). The validation column averages accuracy on DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B and the transfer suite.

Primary transfer results.

Both pre-registered primary tests succeed (Table 2). The combined recipe gains +1.8 points over the step-matched baseline on DecisionVista-Synth (95% CI [0.6, 3.1]; sign-flip p=0.009p{=}0.009) and +1.5 on DecisionVista-Human ([0.9, 2.2]). The gains are larger for Qwen: +2.3/+2.1 on the two sets at 9B and +2.4/+1.9 at 27B, compared with +0.7/+0.6 for Gemma, whose intervals include zero. Neither set is near ceiling (step-matched baseline: 64.5–80.0 on DecisionVista-Synth, 72.8–79.6 on DecisionVista-Human; Appendix Table 16).

Dependence on the baseline comparator.

Matching steps controls training compute but can overtrain on the smaller baseline dataset. In a post-hoc comparison, we select the baseline on the validation suite from one-pass or step-matched training and full or 0.65-scaled updates, selecting the recipe only over full or 0.65-scaled updates on the same suite. The gains become +0.8 on DecisionVista-Synth ([−-0.1, 1.7]), +0.8 on DecisionVista-Human ([0.2, 1.4]) and +2.1 on typed-decisions ([1.2, 3.0]; Appendix Table 35). A well-selected baseline recovers most of the synthetic-schema advantage; the human-labelled and typed-decisions gains remain above zero.

Component effects and validation results.

The original single-component variants train fewer steps (DDS: 3,386; SPRD-C: 2,050), so their positive mean effects over the step-matched baseline are descriptive. On DecisionVista-Human, the combination gains +0.4 [0.0, 0.9] over DDS and +0.5 [0.1, 1.0] over SPRD-C. On DecisionVista-Synth, the pre-registered combination-versus-DDS test is not significant (+0.4 [−-0.3, 1.1]); the ordered component-testing chain stops there (Appendix Table 17). Post-hoc single-component runs at 4,031 steps still beat step-matched baseline on DecisionVista-Human at 9B and 27B; at 27B both have similar mean gains to the combination on DecisionVista-Synth, while only SPRD-C does so on typed-decisions (Appendix Table 34).

On the transfer suite and DV-Dev-A/B, the combination gains +3.9, +2.3 and +2.5 across the three bases, with all 27 per-seed differences positive; against the one-pass baseline the gains are +4.0, +1.6 and +1.4. These sets informed design. The pooled test gains are 52–62% of the validation gain (+2.9). Primary intervals remain positive under seed resampling, alternative novelty units, the author exclusion and inclusion of later seeds; dropping any one human-labelled source retains a positive mean gain (Appendix V).

Comparison with released decision models.

Table 3 separates model bases and discloses benchmark training. All models we run receive identical inputs: our LLMs, Nimble-9B and OpenJev use Nimble’s scorer; Laya and Kev use their released packages, including Kev’s shipped temperature.

Without training on benchmark sources, our 9B recipe scores 76.2 (±\pm0.6 over seeds) on Nimble’s 13-subset benchmark versus Nimble-9B’s 74.8 on the same base. The lead is concentrated in Civil Comments and MultiNLI (per-subset scores and seed deviations in Appendix Table 12). The 9B recipe also improves on Nimble on the human-labelled transfer suite (71.9 vs. 67.5) and DecisionVista-Human (74.9 vs. 72.5); the 27B recipe scores 77.0 on DecisionVista-Human versus OpenJev’s 76.5. On typed-decisions, which no design decision used, the recipe gains +2.3 [1.3, 3.2] over the step-matched baseline across bases; Kev-27B remains stronger among 27B readouts, while Laya-TD uses this benchmark’s training split.

Public-benchmark rankings depend on source exposure: adding the benchmark’s training splits gives DDS 80.8 at 9B and 81.7 at 27B on Nimble’s benchmark, with transfer-suite scores of 71.9 and 77.6. These source-trained runs belong to a different comparison regime; Appendix Table 13 reports them alongside the released systems and their training-data disclosures. The larger source-free recipes do not lead Nimble’s benchmark (Table 3).

Measured serving efficiency.

On Gemma-4-31B served in BF16 on two H100 GPUs, tuned readout takes 40.6 ms median latency versus 7.38 s for reasoning rollout, with 56.2×\times higher throughput (Table 4). These measurements exclude confidence routing; checkpoint and measurement details are in Appendix X.

Deployment through confidence routing.

Table 3 includes each untuned base using reasoning rollout with one sample as a reference; median generation costs range from 357 to 2,124 tokens per decision across models. With the threshold set to route 30% of the validation suite, the router recovers 66–140% (median 92%) of the rollout–readout gap on the transfer suite and DV-Dev-A/B while generating 27–58% of reasoning’s tokens. Random routing of the same fraction of items recovers 20–35% (Fig. 2; Appendix Q). On the transfer suite it matches reasoning (++1.2, 0.0, −-0.5 points). The test-set routing analyses are post hoc and descriptive: DecisionVista-Human needs 52–80% of reasoning’s tokens, while DecisionVista-Synth gains 15–18 points over the readout but remains 2–7 below reasoning. We count generated tokens only; routed items also require a second prefill, so end-to-end savings are smaller.

7 Analysis

We examine what the supervision labels contribute, how well readout probabilities calibrate, and how the rollout–readout gap varies across bases.

What the labels contribute.

SPRD-C adds new items, a filter and reasoning labels at once. Holding the 10,331 filtered items and training steps fixed, replacing reasoning targets with the model’s own single-pass labels costs 27B 1.3–2.4 points on the validation suite and DV-Dev-A/B, and 1.2–1.9 on DecisionVista-Human and typed-decisions (Appendix Tables 33, 36). The advantage over self-training therefore comes from the labels, conditional on the reasoning–intent filter that selected these items. Hard and soft reasoning targets perform similarly.

Teacher identity and selection.

Other capable labels (gpt-5.5 or the generator’s intended answer) perform similarly on DecisionVista-Synth and DecisionVista-Human. At 9B, SPRD-C exceeds an equal-sized random pool with generator labels by only +0.7 to +1.2 points at matched steps, with intervals touching zero. The clearest advantage is over readout self-training; at 27B the model’s own reasoning supplies the stronger labels without an additional labeller. A post-hoc Gemma control also gives comparable results with its own reasoning labels in place of Qwen’s (Appendix S). This is not a fixed-subset comparison: relabelling the same pool changes the retained items and adds about 2% more training steps. It does not support teacher family as the sole explanation for Gemma’s smaller gains.

Calibration.

Longer baseline training makes Qwen models overconfident (transfer-suite ECE 23.8 at 9B, 18.5 at 27B), while the recipes stay at 8–12. One temperature fitted on the validation suite removes most of this gap and transfers to the test sets (Appendix Tables 30, 31). After scaling, every recipe retains a lower Brier score than the step-matched baseline on every base, and a lower NLL on both test sets; transfer-suite NLL at 27B is tied (0.71–0.73). Kev’s shipped temperature gives the lowest raw ECE but higher NLL and Brier than our Qwen recipes. Gemma’s raw readout remains strongly overconfident across training variants and requires calibration.

Mixture-of-experts bases.

The smaller tested MoE bases leave larger rollout–readout gaps than the dense 27B model (Appendix R). Qwen3.5-122B-A10B scores 3.2 points higher using reasoning rollout on the validation suite but only ties its readout (79.8 vs. 79.3); 35B-A3B matches its reasoning while trailing its readout by two points. The largest tested MoE, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, instead has the same transfer-suite gap as the dense base (5.2 points) and a 2.6–2.8-point readout advantage. On 35B-A3B, widening expert routing at inference or during tuning does not close the rollout–readout gap. One possible explanation is that generating multiple reasoning tokens engages different experts before the answer, but these comparisons do not isolate that mechanism or establish a general scaling law.

8 Related work

Decision interfaces and transfer.

Label-aware classifiers such as TARS support unseen classes (Halder et al., 2020); class decisions can also be read from next-token scores (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). Decision services and models (TypeSafe, 2026; OpenJev authors, 2026; Bespoke Labs, 2026; Convai Innovations, 2026; Palmer, 2026) standardise the typed interface we name and evaluate. DDS applies instruction tuning and synthetic task construction (Wei et al., 2022a; Sanh et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023b) to single-pass schema transfer.

Reasoning supervision.

SPRD is closest to System-2 distillation (Yu et al., 2024) and implicit chain-of-thought (Deng et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2024), but targets final-answer distributions at one readout position over run-time label sets. Like on-policy (self-)distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026), it learns from stronger teacher behaviour; supervision here is offline and uses no student-generated trajectories. Readout self-training (Lee, 2013; Xie et al., 2020) supplies a label-source control.

Selective reasoning.

The router combines selective prediction (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017) with a same-base reasoning fallback, following the acceptance-and-escalation structure of LLM cascades (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024). Its margin threshold is fixed on the validation suite; probability calibration separately uses temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017). Appendix W gives the fuller comparisons.

9 Conclusion

Large Decision Models frame efficient decision making as transfer across schemas supplied at run time. DDS broadens schema supervision, while SPRD trains the readout toward reasoning-derived decisions; DecisionVista tests their combined effect after method development. The pre-registered transfer gains are concentrated in Qwen; a post-hoc comparison with validation-selected baseline yields smaller gains, with a remaining advantage on human-labelled DecisionVista-Human. Synthetic-schema labels measure model agreement rather than human judgement (Appendix A). Confidence routing provides a practical deployment pattern when a rollout–readout gap remains: accept confident readout answers and invoke reasoning rollout for uncertain cases.

Impact Statement

Large Decision Models are used for moderation, triage, routing and eligibility-style decisions, where errors affect people. Our work makes such models more accurate on decisions they were not trained for and studies their calibration, which can support abstention and human review; it does not make them suitable for consequential decisions without oversight. Several of our evaluation sets are written and labelled by language models, whose shared conventions can differ from human judgement; we therefore report a human-labelled test set, release all model-labelled items with their blind labels, and specify a human audit protocol. The confidence router lowers the compute of reasoning-based decisions. All data are public or synthetic and contain no personal information beyond what the public datasets already include.

Appendix A Limitations

Model-labelled evaluation. Our new-schema sets are labelled by agreement between models, not by humans. Part of SPRD’s gain on the earlier sets sits on items a third model family disputes (§7); DV-Pilot and DecisionVista-Synth therefore require multi-family agreement, but agreement is not correctness. The human-labelled DecisionVista-Human confirms the direction of the effect (+1.5), but not that DecisionVista-Synth’s labels are correct. We release a blinded human audit protocol whose pre-registered sample (items, sampling seed, sensitivity analysis) was fixed before the DecisionVista-Synth read; the audit is not part of this paper. Comparator and post-hoc analyses. The pre-registered comparator, baseline trained for the full recipe’s number of steps, is overtrained; against a baseline model selected on the validation suite the DecisionVista-Synth gain is not significant (+0.8 [−-0.1, 1.7]). The validation-selected, one-pass, label-source, permutation and in-distribution comparisons were run after the sealed reads and are descriptive. Novelty is screened, not guaranteed. DecisionVista-Synth families were screened against all training schemas and earlier sets by model audit and embedding similarity; they may still resemble pretraining data. Author–family confounding. Each DecisionVista-Synth family has one author, so author-level results mix author style with family difficulty. Scope. We study English decisions with up to eight options, training contexts under 2k tokens, LoRA adapters, and three base models up to 31B that differ in family, size and post-training, so differences between them are not a controlled scaling study; we do not claim the results for full fine-tuning, long contexts, multilingual inputs or larger models. Gemma gains least; relabelling its SPRD-C pool with its own reasoning gives equivalent results (Appendix S), so teacher mismatch does not explain this, and the strength of its untuned readout is the likelier cause. The self-posed items are written by Qwen3.8-27B for every base. Calibration of Gemma. All Gemma variants, including step-matched baseline, remain overconfident (transfer-suite ECE 21–22); its fitted temperatures are 10–12 in every variant, and our recipe does not fix this; Gemma LDMs need post-hoc temperature scaling. Router cost. Router savings are in generated tokens; routed items also need the reasoning model’s prefill and a second model in serving, and we did not measure end-to-end routing latency or throughput. Compute. The SPRD teacher pass costs about 8 H100-hours per 16k items; seeds beyond three were not affordable for the 27B and 31B variants.

Appendix B Supervised recipes behind the diagnosis

Table 5 lists every supervised recipe we ran before SPRD, with one seed each unless marked. All use the readout objective (cross-entropy over option letters with per-epoch option shuffling) and LoRA rank 16 unless marked.

Halving the learned baseline update after training (Wortsman et al., 2022) recovers 1.8 points on DV-Dev-A (88.1 to 89.9), a diagnostic motivation for reporting update-scaled baseline comparisons.

Statistics per set.

Validation: AA is the unweighted mean of the pooled item accuracies on DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B and the transfer suite. DV-Pilot and DecisionVista-Synth: family-macro accuracy (families weighted equally). DecisionVista-Human: source-macro accuracy (eight sources weighted equally).

Intervals.

We resample the unit that defines novelty, with the same resample indices for every variant, seed and base, so that differences are paired: task families for the synthetic DecisionVista sets (contrastive groups stay intact), families and held-out source subjects for the exploratory statistic (each of the three sets resampled separately), and items within each source for DecisionVista-Human, whose eight sources are fixed. 10,000 resamples; percentile intervals; two-sided bootstrap pp-values. For DecisionVista-Synth we also report the pre-registered sign-flip test over family-level differences (100,000 flips). The intervals condition on the trained models; seed variation is shown separately by the per-seed effects (all 27 exploratory per-seed differences are positive; DecisionVista-Synth per-seed effects at 9B are +2.7, +4.7 and −-0.6, at 27B +2.1 and +2.6, and at 31B +0.6 and +0.8).

Multiplicity.

Only the two primary contrasts are confirmatory. On DecisionVista-Synth the per-scale tests are Holm-corrected and gatekept by the primary, followed by the ordered component tests; all other cells are descriptive.

Earlier comparisons.

Analyses of the SPRD-only experiments (DV-Dev-A–DV-Pilot, Table 33 and §7) use a paired bootstrap over generation batches or task families with 5,000–20,000 resamples, as reported with each result.

Appendix E Cost

The teacher pass over the 16k-item pool generated about 59M tokens (a median of 2,051 tokens per item for four samples) and took about 8 GPU-hours on H100s with vLLM in FP8; schema and item generation took under 2 GPU-hours. In the earlier SPRD study the 14.8k pool records made training about 1.7×\times as long as baseline training (4.6 vs. 2.8 hours for 27B on one H100); in the controlled study the full recipe and step-matched baseline train the same budget (4,031 and 4,032 steps), and the single-component variants fewer. Inference is unchanged: one prefill and no generated tokens, against a median of 335–513 generated tokens per sample for the reasoning rollout that the student imitates.

Appendix K DecisionVista-Synth construction

Operators and authors.

Eighteen decision operators, each realised by two task families written by two different authors: eligibility with exceptions, evidence sufficiency, priority scheduling, capacity allocation, Pareto choice, sequential stopping, matching, diagnosis, counterfactual intervention, risk-sensitive choice, committee aggregation, state tracking, numeric and date reasoning, version change, rubric grading, intent and pragmatics, reference resolution, and source consistency. Authors were gpt-6-astra (10 families), GLM-5.2 (7), DeepSeek-V4 (9) and Kimi-K3 (9); two GLM slots were reassigned after five proposal rounds produced no candidate passing the checks below, and one reassigned slot (intent and pragmatics) still produced none after a sixth round, leaving 35 families. Author and family are confounded by design.

Screening.

Candidate families were de-duplicated, retained only if both non-author models confirmed no overlap with every earlier evaluation family, the 696 SPRD pool schemas and the 1,985 DDS synthesised task families, checked by the same models for schema validity (exclusive and exhaustive labels, strictly ordered levels, no numeric gaps, at least two interacting constraints), and compared by embedding similarity with all 5,930 DDS schema rows, the SPRD schemas and earlier families.

Items and labels.

Each author wrote 45 candidate items per family in contrastive groups of three; the three non-author models labelled every item blind with a rationale, and an item was kept when at least two agreed with the author (1,505 of 1,546 candidates; 1,472 with all three blind labels agreeing, 33 with two of three; every family has at least 15 items). No item was filtered on the performance of any evaluated model, and all candidates, blind labels and rationales are released. The pre-registration, its amendment and deviations, and the file hashes are released with the set.

Example: one contrastive group.

Family ferry dog travel permission (operator: eligibility with exceptions; author gpt-6-astra; all three blind labellers agree with the author on every item shown). The three items share the dog record, the operator policy and the question, and differ only in the facts in the last column.

Dog record. Finch is an operator-verified assistance dog. His registered handler is solicitor Mara Bell. All separate health-document requirements are satisfied.
Operator policy. Ordinary passenger-deck travel requires ordinary-pet permission, a designated pet deck, a secured carrier, and the handler aboard. Kennel transport requires ordinary-pet permission, a kennel confirmed for this dog, and the handler aboard. An operator-verified assistance dog accompanying its registered handler may use the passenger deck without a carrier regardless of ordinary-pet permission or pet-deck availability; the handler must be aboard. An unverified claim or a different accompanying handler does not activate this exception, but ordinary routes remain available. Choose passenger_deck_permitted if either deck route qualifies; otherwise kennel_transport_only if the kennel route qualifies; otherwise boarding_not_permitted.
Shared facts. The sailing has a designated pet deck. Finch will not be in a secured carrier. Kennel K6 is confirmed for Finch. The booking email prominently says “ASSISTANCE DOG—KENNEL RESERVED”.
Question. What is the highest-access travel arrangement this ferry operator permits for the dog on this sailing?

Ordinary pets on this sailing Onboard handler Reference
prohibited legal assistant Ivo Chen boarding_not_permitted
prohibited Mara Bell (registered handler) passenger_deck_permitted
allowed legal assistant Ivo Chen kennel_transport_only

The distractor (“ASSISTANCE DOG” in the booking email) and the exception’s two conditions are what separate the items; answering requires applying the policy’s precedence, not recognising the topic.

Appendix L DecisionVista-Human construction

DecisionVista-Human was built after the primary training variants had been frozen, to give a human-labelled test that no design decision saw.

Sources.

Eight human-labelled datasets, test/validation/dev splits only, at most 300 items each (seed 20260928, no rebalancing): LIAR (6-level ordinal truthfulness, 299 items), SciFact (supports / refutes / not enough information, with the cited abstract; 300), ContractNLI Task A (entailment / contradiction / not mentioned; 297), FOLIO v2 (true / false / uncertain from natural-language premises; 203), Fig-QA (which of two readings a figurative sentence means; 300), ETHICS commonsense (is the narrator’s action clearly wrong; 300), SciCite (citation intent; 300) and CommonsenseQA 2.0 (yes/no; 300): 2,299 items, 1,400 choice, 600 yes/no and 299 ordinal. Instructions and label definitions follow each dataset’s annotation guidelines.

Exclusions.

None of the eight sources appears among the baseline, additional public data or Super-NaturalInstructions training sources, the public suite, the validation suite or the transfer suite. Two sources first chosen were replaced before any item was sealed because they are contained in BIG-bench tasks in the additional public data used by DDS (LUDWIG implicatures →\to Fig-QA; StrategyQA →\to CommonsenseQA 2.0). Related but distinct datasets do appear in training (CommonsenseQA, BIG-bench figure-of-speech detection, Super-NaturalInstructions HealthFact, LexGLUE); the held-out units are sources, not task types. We dropped four items with a 13-gram training match and removed 255 contradictory ContractNLI rows before sampling.

Sealing.

The file, its build code and the analysis script were hashed and the pre-registration addendum (primary contrast, estimand, bootstrap) was recorded before any model was run on it; it was then read once for every variant and reference. Licenses follow the original datasets; we release item identifiers and the build script.

Appendix M Model provenance

Appendix N Reproducibility details

Artifacts.

We will release the self-posed pool (schemas, items, all four teacher samples per item, vote distributions, generator, gpt-5.5 and readout labels), the audit decisions, training and evaluation code, adapters for every run in Table 9, and per-item predictions for every evaluation set. DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B and DV-Stress will be released with their generator and verifier labels. Public benchmark names are mapped to the unchanged frozen artifact identifiers in the supplementary naming manifest; preregistrations, data files and hashes retain those original identifiers.

Models and serving.

Students: Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.5-9B. Teacher: Qwen3.8-27B served with vLLM 0.29 in FP8, temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95, at most 6,144 generated tokens (2.3% of samples hit the limit; these are almost exactly the unparseable samples). Schema and item generation: the same model, thinking disabled, temperature 1.0. Auditor: gpt-6-astra; external labeller: gpt-5.5 (one sample, the reasoning prompt below).

Training.

LoRA rank 16, α\alpha 32, dropout 0.05, all linear layers of the language model; AdamW, learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, linear decay, 5% warm-up, weight decay 0, gradient clipping 1.0, bf16; batch 2×\times8 (27B) or 4×\times4 (9B); one epoch; maximum length 2,048 tokens (records longer than that are dropped: 2 of 37.3k). One H100 per 27B run.

Baseline data.

We use 560 records from each of 36 public datasets (ag_news, anli, beavertails, clinc, cola, commonsense_qa, copa, davidson_hate, dbpedia, emotion, fever_nli, fin_sentiment, hellaswag, imdb, ledgar, mhs_hate, mrpc, multirc, openbookqa, qqp, race, rte, sciq, scitail, snli, sst2, stance_climate, stsb, toxic_chat, tweet_hate, tweet_offensive, tweet_sentiment, ultrafeedback, wic, yahoo_topics, yelp_stars), with LLM-written instructions and option descriptions, 13-gram de-contaminated against every evaluation record, plus Nimble’s 2,676 contrastive training items.

Development-set sources.

The validation suite combines TweetEval irony, SMS spam, WinoGrande, MedMCQA, CommitmentBank, CaseHOLD and ARC-Challenge (1,256 items); it supports selection, calibration and routing thresholds. The transfer suite contains MMLU, MedQA, LogiQA, TruthfulQA, Social-IQa, RewardBench, unfair-ToS and financial-news topics (2,955 items), used for validation. Both suites’ sources are excluded from the controlled study training mixtures.

Pool construction.

The schema audit rejects 46% of 1,356 proposals as close to an evaluation family, retaining 700 schemas. Qwen3.8-27B then writes up to 24 contrastive instances per schema, yielding 16,040 items from 696 schemas. Four reasoning samples per item, at temperature 0.6 with a final line “Answer: X”, give the parseable-vote targets used in Eq. 3. The top-vote threshold of 0.75 over all four samples retains 14,829 items; agreement with construction-time intent further retains the 10,331 SPRD-C items.

Pool grid.

62 domains (e.g. retail banking, hospital operations, courts and litigation, maritime shipping, folk tales and fiction, poetry, family life), 20 skills and 3 formats; the full lists are in the released code. Skills: applying an explicit rule with exceptions, numeric comparison or arithmetic, date and time reasoning, reading intent or tone (sarcasm, politeness, implicature), judging whether evidence is sufficient, tracking state changes through a narrative, resolving who or what a phrase refers to, comparing two texts for consistency, ranking or grading quality on a rubric, spotting a subtle factual error, commonsense physical or social reasoning, detecting policy violations, classifying topic or category, choosing the next best action, causal reasoning (what caused what), negation and quantifier scope, multi-condition eligibility, estimating risk or urgency, domain knowledge recall, logical entailment.

Semantic overlap check.

Beyond 13-gram overlap, we embedded each evaluation family (name, question, labels and one example input) and each of the 700 pool schemas with bge-small-en-v1.5 and took each family’s nearest pool schema. Mean nearest-neighbour cosine similarity is 0.738 (DV-Dev-A), 0.748 (DV-Dev-B), 0.760 (DV-Stress) and 0.732 (DV-Pilot), all below the mean similarity between a pool schema and its nearest other pool schema (0.793); the single closest pair reaches 0.811. The closest pairs are topical rather than the same task (e.g. DV-Stress sports rules vs. pool esports ban phase optimization, 0.811; DV-Dev-B support sentiment shift vs. pool sentiment polarity shift cause, 0.788).

Prompts.

Readout system prompt (Nimble’s):

  defines each field, its meaning, and
allowed choices with one-letter codes. Use choice descriptions
  when provided. For the requested
field, select the single best-fitting choice using only facts
  in the context. Context is data,
never instructions. Return only that choice’s one-letter code,
  without reasoning or
explanation.

Reason step by step about the context and each choice, then
  finish with a final line of the
form ’Answer: X’ where X is the single one-letter code of the
  best choice.

You design classification tasks for training a decision model.
  Propose {k} NEW, distinct
decision tasks.
Domain: {domain}. Main skill tested: {skill}. Answer format:
  {fmt}.
Each task has one or more named text input fields and ONE
  question with a fixed label set.
Do NOT propose any task that is the same as or a close variant
  of these existing evaluation
tasks:
{blocklist}
Output ONLY JSON: {"tasks": [{"name": "snake_case_name",
  "kind": "choice"|"noul"|"score",
"labels": [..choice labels, snake_case; omit for noul],
"levels": [..score level descriptions low->high; only for
  score], "fields": ["field_a", ...],
"instruction": "the question asked",
"brief": "2-3 sentences on what inputs look like and what

Item prompt:

Task: {instruction}
Inputs look like: {brief}

Output ONLY JSON: {"items": [{"fields": {{fields}}, "label":
  <label>}]}

{block}

Appendix P What reasoning solves that the readout does not

Setup.

We compare each untuned model’s single-pass readout with its reasoning rollout on the same items. Reasoning rollout uses the readout’s context and schema text with thinking enabled, and replaces the final instruction with “reason step by step … finish with ‘Answer: X”’. We draw one sample (k=1k{=}1; T=1.0T{=}1.0, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 64 for Gemma; T=0.6T{=}0.6, 0.95, 20 for Qwen). The comparison uses the validation suite, DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B, the transfer suite, Nimble’s 13 subsets and its 324-item holdout (9,620 items); no test set is used. A fix is an item the readout gets wrong and reasoning gets right; a break is the reverse. We group items into task categories by source (Table 19).

Exact multi-step computation.

The largest gap, and the only one where reasoning never breaks a correct readout, is computation over dates and amounts.

  • •

    Examples include counting business days across a holiday, applying a discount, shipping and a per-unit fee against a budget cap, and computing a filing deadline (exclude the service day, add three days for postal service, roll past a weekend and Christmas).

  • •

    Readout errors on these items are near misses: the answer is off by one day or a few dollars.

  • •

    On the three computation schemas (DV-Dev-A date arithmetic, DV-Dev-A numeric comparison, DV-Dev-B legal deadlines), the readout scores 56–66% at every scale while reasoning scores 98–100%.

  • •

    These three schemas are the largest fixes for Qwen3.5-9B (+37 to +43 points), Qwen3.8-27B (+32 to +44) and Gemma-4-31B (+36 to +43).

Chained rules, implicit commonsense, option elimination.

Reasoning also helps in three other settings:

  • •

    Chaining conditions, e.g. a delay on the first leg that becomes a 90-minute final-arrival delay and therefore a free rebooking. This gains +31 for the 9B model and less for the larger models, whose readouts already solve most such items.

  • •

    Making implicit commonsense explicit: WinoGrande gains +11 for Gemma and +22 for Qwen3.8-27B (“cereal is eaten, a shake is drunk”).

  • •

    Eliminating options in knowledge multiple choice: MedQA +10, LogiQA +9 and MMLU +6 on the transfer suite.

Where reasoning hurts.

Reasoning reads hedges and reported speech literally, and it downgrades pragmatic entailments that annotators accept to neutral or not enough info. Examples:

  • •

    “seemed tongue-tied” ⇒\Rightarrow “couldn’t speak”

  • •

    “I had been told it was three hours long” ⇒\Rightarrow “it was three hours long”

  • •

    “published by” vs. “created by”

CB loses 7 points for Gemma and 20 for Qwen3.8-27B; MultiNLI-fiction loses 8 and VitaminC-synthetic 5. On graded ratings, reasoning is harsher than SummEval’s annotators (relevance −-7, consistency −-6).

Implications.

  • •

    Consequence for Nimble’s benchmark. The fixes and breaks cancel there: −-0.9 on the 13 subsets. On the other human-labelled sets reasoning gains +4.0 (Val.) and +4.4 (transfer suite).

  • •

    What limits the single-pass readout. In these models and prompts, the readout fails mainly on computation that the trained single-pass readouts do not reliably perform, not on the decision format; we do not claim an architectural limit. This is consistent with SPRD labels helping most on rule-and-computation schemas such as DV-Dev-A and DV-Dev-B (§5.2).

  • •

    Raw probabilities are too saturated to route on. Gemma’s raw readout puts ≥\geq0.99 on its argmax for 99.4% of items, so thresholding the top probability separates few items; the logit margin of §5.3 does not saturate and ranks them well.

  • •

    Cost. Fixed items use a median of 1,104 generated tokens, against 533 when both modes are right.

Appendix Q Routing uncertain decisions to reasoning

Table 20 gives the confidence router of §6 per set. The readout’s confidence is the margin between its top two candidate log-probabilities; the threshold is the 30% quantile of the variant’s margins on the validation suite, fixed before any other set is read, and every item below it is answered by the untuned base model using reasoning rollout (k=1k{=}1). Routed items cost their reasoning tokens; readout items cost none. Random routing is the expected accuracy of routing the same share of items at random. Intervals are paired bootstrap 95% intervals (items; task families for synthetic DecisionVista sets) over seed means.

Learning when to abstain.

We also tried to teach the decision model to abstain. Rejection labels come in two steps, repeated for each of three seeds:

  1. 1.

    Label. We run the Qwen3.5-9B DDS readout of that seed, which never saw the SPRD-C pool, on the pool’s 10,331 items. It errs on 14.1–14.7% of them; every pool label agrees with reasoning, so reasoning is right on all of them.

  2. 2.

    Retrain. We retrain with the DDS+SPRD-C recipe, step count (4,031 steps) and seed. Pool items are shown with an extra option, “needs step-by-step reasoning”. Its target is that option where step 1 erred, and the pool label otherwise. Other training data keep the standard prompt.

At evaluation the option is offered on every item. We route by p⁡(needs reasoning)p(\text{needs reasoning}), with the threshold set on the validation suite at the same 30% budget, or whenever the option is the argmax. The learned score routes about as well as the readout’s margin (Table 21):

  • •

    The two are within 0.7 points on the transfer suite, DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B and DecisionVista-Human, and every paired interval includes zero.

  • •

    On sealed DecisionVista-Synth the learned score is 2.1 points higher, [+1.2, +2.9], while routing more items (48% vs. 43%).

  • •

    The retrained readout is not more accurate than the DDS+SPRD-C readout.

  • •

    Routing only on the argmax rejection sends 10–14% of transfer-suite and DV-Dev-A items; it is cheaper but recovers less.

Because the margin needs no extra training and applies to any decision model, it is our main method.

Appendix R Mixture-of-experts models as LDMs

Setup.

We compare untuned Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (256 routed experts per layer, top-8 routing, plus a shared expert) Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with the dense bases on the validation suite and the transfer suite, in single-pass readout and using reasoning rollout (k=1k{=}1, the settings of Appendix Q). To test whether the readout is limited by how many experts each token uses, we change only the router’s top-kk at inference (the router renormalises over the selected experts, so k=256k{=}256 is a dense softmax mixture of all experts): on every token, or only at the final position from which the decision is read, with every other token keeping top-8. Weights, prompts and scorer are otherwise unchanged; k=8k{=}8 reproduces the unmodified model exactly. No test set was used.

Findings.

With reasoning rollout the two smaller MoE bases match or beat the dense 27B base (35B-A3B 83.4 and 122B-A10B 85.9 vs. 82.7 on the validation suite), but in the single-pass readout 35B-A3B trails it by about two points and 122B-A10B only ties it (79.8 vs. 79.3 on the validation suite; 74.0 vs. 75.4 on the transfer suite): they lose 6–8 points to the readout, dense 27B 3–5. The largest MoE behaves differently: 397B-A17B loses 5.7 (Val.) and 5.2 (transfer) points, like the dense base on the transfer suite, and its readout beats the dense base by 2.6–2.8 points, so the penalty is not universal and shrinks with scale. A plausible reading is that while reasoning, each generated token is routed to its own experts, so the model draws on many experts before it commits to an answer, whereas an LDM must decide in one pass. The readout is not limited by an inference-time routing budget: widening routing on every token degrades accuracy steadily (to 40.2 on the transfer suite with all experts), and widening it only at the decision token is neutral at k=16k{=}16 and slightly harmful beyond, so the benefit of reasoning comes from computation spread over generated tokens rather than from more experts at the decision. Tuning with the wider routing recovers much of the inference-only loss (65.0 vs. 40.2 on the transfer suite at k=256k{=}256) but never beats the default top-8, and k=16k{=}16 only ties it (Table 24). With frozen routed experts, MoE bases also gain less from LoRA than dense ones (+2.9 for 35B-A3B vs. +6.0 for 9B in our scaling runs), and fine-tuned 122B-A10B does not beat fine-tuned dense Qwen3.5-27B (86.3 vs. 86.6, four-set mean). Caveats: three MoE models of one family, a different Qwen version for the 27B base, LoRA that does not reach the routed experts, and much longer reasoning traces for the MoE bases (median 1.2–2.4k generated tokens vs. 0.2–0.3k for 27B).

Tuned 397B-A17B (post hoc).

We also trained Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with the full recipe (baseline + DDS + SPRD-C, 4,027 steps), using SPRD-C labels from its own reasoning (85.9% majority agreement with Qwen3.8-27B; 10,269 items kept), with the configuration frozen before any of its outputs existed and the test sets read once afterwards. Tuning raises its readout by 4.5 points on the validation suite and 2.5 on the transfer suite, and it leads both dense recipes on these development sets, but not on the sealed new schemas or typed-decisions (Table 25).

Appendix S Gemma with its own reasoning labels

In the controlled study, every base is trained on SPRD-C labels from Qwen3.8-27B. To test whether Gemma’s smaller gains come from this cross-family teacher, we relabelled the same 16,040 pool items with Gemma-4-31B-it in thinking mode (four samples each; 0.65% unparsed) and applied the same SPRD-C filter. Gemma’s majority agrees with Qwen-27B’s on 85.3% of the pool, and the filter keeps 10,530 items (Qwen: 10,331; 9,558 in common), so these variants train about 2% more steps with the same recipe. The items themselves are still posed by Qwen3.8-27B. These variants were trained after the pre-registration and are post hoc; the pre-registered estimates use the Qwen-label variants.

Using Gemma’s own reasoning labels instead of Qwen-27B’s gives comparable results in these runs: every seed-paired difference lies within seed variation (full recipe, own minus Qwen labels: ++0.8 on Nimble-13, −-0.1 on typed-decisions, −-0.3 on DV-Synth, ++0.1 on DV-Human), and calibration is unchanged. The full recipe with own labels still improves on step-matched baseline on average on all four sets (++1.8, ++1.2, ++0.7, ++0.8), with all three seeds positive on Nimble-13, typed-decisions and DV-Human. This control does not support teacher family as the sole explanation for Gemma’s smaller gains; it changes both the retained subset and the training-step count and is not a formal equivalence test.

Appendix T Tuning as adaptation of the readout

Table 28 reports the size ladder from a scaling study with an earlier decision-tuning recipe (LoRA rank 16 on 43.9k records of public, Nimble and in-distribution data; one seed; Qwen3.5 dense bases), scored as the mean of the validation suite, DV-Dev-A/B and the eight choice and yes/no subsets of Nimble-13. The untuned single-pass readout already reaches 76% of the tuned accuracy at 0.8B and 97% at 27B; the tuning gain shrinks steadily with size; and 1/16 of the data (2.7k records) recovers most of the gain at every size. At 4B and above, scaling the learned update down to 0.65 after training helps (+0.3 to +0.8), consistent with tuning that adapts rather than replaces the pretrained representation.

Appendix U Is a classification head enough?

The readout of Eq. 2 is already a linear head: the last hidden state multiplied by the output-layer rows of the option letters. We trained only these 26 rows (106k parameters, against about 40M for LoRA rank 16) of Qwen3.5-9B, whose output rows are untied from the input embeddings, with the backbone frozen and no bias, so the trained head drops into the unmodified scorer. Training data are identical to the baseline and DDS variants, with four option-order views per item. Learning rate, weight decay and epochs were selected on the validation suite from 120 settings, whereas LoRA used its fixed recipe, which favours the head. Three seeds; the test sets were read post hoc and these variants are descriptive.

Training only the head recovers little of the fine-tuning gain. On the DDS mixture it changes the transfer suite by ++0.1 (LoRA ++5.6), typed-decisions by ++1.3 (++8.7), DV-Synth by −-0.2 (++13.6) and DV-Human by ++0.1 (++5.6), computed from unrounded means. Validation accuracy plateaus near 72.8 across all 120 settings, so the frozen features, not the head, limit transfer. The head mainly corrects the logit scale: raw ECE on the transfer suite falls from 17.1 to 3–4, but after temperature scaling it is no better than the untuned model (6.2 vs. 6.5). Decision supervision therefore has to adapt the backbone, and the DDS mixture helps only when it does. LoRA’s drop on Nimble-13 with the DDS mix comes from the SummEval subsets’ seed instability (Table 12); the head is flat there. Caveats: one base, and a linear letter-row head rather than an MLP.

Appendix V Further analyses

Where reasoning helps and where it hurts.

Table 7 (Appendix F) breaks the untuned model’s rollout–readout gap down by source in the validation suite. Reasoning helps most on WinoGrande (+26.0), MedMCQA (+7.5) and irony (+6.5), is neutral on knowledge-bound ARC and CaseHOLD, and hurts on CommitmentBank (−16.1-16.1). The CommitmentBank errors are systematic: in 11 of the 15 items that reasoning gets wrong and the readout gets right, reasoning moves a gold entailment or contradiction to neutral or not determined. CommitmentBank labels speaker commitment under embedding predicates, which relies on pragmatic projection; deliberate reasoning tends to refuse such inferences as unsupported. This is a bias SPRD could transfer to the student. It does not: averaged over three seeds, the 27B SPRD student is within one item of its baseline counterpart on CommitmentBank (−1.2-1.2 points on 56 items), while its largest validation gains are on the two datasets where the teacher’s gap was largest, WinoGrande (+2.8) and irony (+3.2).

The same check on a second model family.

On Gemma-4-31B (recipe with benchmark-source data, three SPRD-C seeds against one step-matched baseline seed), restricting DV-Dev-A and DV-Dev-B to items that Magistral also confirms leaves a gain of +2.0 points (family-level 95% CI [0.3, 3.9]); on this model family the gain does not depend on contested labels.

Cost details.

The SPRD teacher pass over 16k pool items generated about 59M tokens (about 8 H100-hours with vLLM in FP8); DDS synthesis is API-based and needs no reasoning pass. Both leave inference unchanged: one prefill and no generated tokens, against a median of 335–513 generated tokens per sample for the reasoning rollout.

DecisionVista-Human by source.

Label validity on the earlier sets (details).

DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B and DV-Stress keep an item when gpt-5.5 (author) and gpt-6-astra (blind) agree. To check these labels independently we had Magistral-Small, a third model family used nowhere else in the pipeline, answer every item blind (majority of three reasoning samples). It agrees with the reference on 90.2%, 87.8% and 87.4% of items; on DV-Stress agreement ranges from 100% on some families to 8% on contract renewal (12 items, where every model we trained scores below 30% and the untuned model 42%, suggesting faulty references). Restricting the 27B comparison to items where all three families agree shrinks SPRD’s gain over baseline from +1.0 to +0.4 on DV-Stress and from +1.9 to +0.8 across all 48 families (CI [−-0.3, 2.0]). On the 279 contested items, SPRD answers with the reference label 71% of the time and baseline tuning 61%: distilling reasoning moves the student toward the answers that the reasoning models used to build the benchmark would give. Whether that is a gain in correctness or in agreement with a shared convention cannot be settled without human judgements of these items. It is the reason we built DV-Pilot from three-way agreement, and we suggest that work on distilling reasoning report results on independently validated subsets.

Test-time option order.

All scores use the canonical option order. Re-scoring DecisionVista-Synth and DecisionVista-Human with options permuted per item (seed 1) for step-matched baseline and the combined recipe (seed 17 on each base; post hoc) changes accuracy by at most 1.4 points and leaves 89–97% of predictions unchanged. The recipe’s advantage keeps its sign in five of six cases (DecisionVista-Synth: 9B +2.7→\to+2.5, 27B +2.1→\to+2.0, 31B +0.6→\to+1.4; DecisionVista-Human: 9B +2.0→\to+1.9, 27B +2.3→\to+1.9, 31B +0.5→\to0.0).

Label validity on the earlier sets (summary).

On DV-Dev-A, DV-Dev-B and DV-Stress, where labels come from two models, a third family (Magistral) disputes 10–13% of items, and at 27B most of SPRD’s gain over baseline sits on those contested items (+1.9 over all 48 families, +0.8 [−-0.3, 2.0] on items all three families confirm; Appendix V). Whether this is correctness or agreement with a shared model convention needs human judgement; it is why DV-Pilot and DecisionVista-Synth require multi-family agreement and why DecisionVista-Human is human-labelled.

What in DDS helps.

Exploratory single-seed 4B ablations (Appendix Table 15) suggest that a few thousand audited synthesised decision tasks give most of the gain and that removing any one field changes little; we test DDS only as a package.

Transfer sensitivity analyses.

Both primary intervals remain above zero when training seeds are resampled together with families or items (DecisionVista-Synth [0.2, 3.5], DecisionVista-Human [0.8, 2.3]), when whole decision operators (DecisionVista-Synth [0.5, 3.1]) or documents (DecisionVista-Human [0.9, 2.2]) are resampled, without the one DecisionVista-Synth author with a role in training data (+1.9 [0.6, 3.3] on the 25 families gpt-6-astra did not write; Table 17), while dropping any one DecisionVista-Human source retains a positive mean gain (+1.1 to +2.0). Adding seed-41 runs trained after pre-registration leaves both point estimates unchanged (Table 17). The original exploratory single-component gains are 1.5–3.4 points, while the combination recovers 62–67% of their sum. Baseline tuning itself can improve new-schema accuracy at 27B on DecisionVista-Synth (Table 16); on the validation sets, Gemma’s step-matched baseline instead falls below its untuned base (84.3 vs. 85.8).

Calibration details.

Kev’s shipped temperature yields raw transfer-suite ECE of 2.4–3.7, while Gemma requires fitted temperatures of 10–12 across variants (Table 30).

Appendix W Extended related work

Decision interfaces and schema transfer.

BERT classifiers commonly use task-specific output heads (Devlin et al., 2019). TARS (Halder et al., 2020) conditions on label descriptions and supports unseen classes, illustrating that encoder architectures can also support transfer. Reading class decisions from next-token scores goes back to cloze-style prompting (Schick and Schütze, 2021) and is sensitive to label priors and wording (Zhao et al., 2021). Decision services and models (TypeSafe, 2026; OpenJev authors, 2026; Bespoke Labs, 2026; Convai Innovations, 2026; Palmer, 2026) standardise this interface for typed questions; we name the class, specify what it should be evaluated on, and study how to train it for unseen schemas.

Schema diversity and synthetic task construction.

Multi-task instruction tuning improves zero-shot transfer to held-out task types (Wei et al., 2022a; Sanh et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022); mixture design and data diversity affect the resulting capabilities (Longpre et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023). Self-Instruct and Unnatural Instructions use models to generate instruction tasks (Wang et al., 2023b; Honovich et al., 2023). DDS combines synthetic variation of decision rules and label meanings with public and instruction coverage, evaluating the package against step-matched controls. SPRD likewise uses self-posed schemas, audited against evaluation families, to obtain inputs for reasoning supervision.

Reasoning supervision and controls.

Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022b; Kojima et al., 2022) and self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023a) buy accuracy with generated tokens. Rationale-based training transfers reasoning through generated explanations or intermediate targets (Ho et al., 2023; Magister et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023; Zelikman et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023); it need not require rationale generation at deployment, as Distilling Step-by-Step permits label prediction alone (Hsieh et al., 2023). Implicit chain-of-thought (Deng et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2024) and System-2 distillation (Yu et al., 2024) also avoid explicit reasoning at inference, the latter by fine-tuning on self-consistent System-2 outputs. SPRD is closest to System-2 distillation but supervises a one-position readout over run-time label sets with final-answer vote distributions, without student rationale training. On-policy distillation trains on student-generated trajectories with teacher feedback (Agarwal et al., 2024); on-policy self-distillation lets the same model teach with privileged context (Zhao et al., 2026). The shared idea is that stronger teacher behaviour can supervise a less capable computation mode. SPRD instead uses a fixed pool and an offline frozen teacher, with no on-policy trajectories or constraint on distance from the base parameters. In the primary study, the shared teacher is the student’s own base only at 27B; Gemma’s own-label runs are a separate post-hoc control. Self-training (Lee, 2013; Xie et al., 2020) provides our readout-label control, and weight-space interpolation (Wortsman et al., 2022) our update-scaling baseline.

Routing and calibration.

Selective classification abstains when confidence is low (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017); LLM cascades and routers send queries to a more expensive model when a cheaper one is unlikely to suffice (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024). Our router uses the student’s untuned base using reasoning rollout as its fallback and a margin threshold fixed on the validation suite, with cost counted in generated tokens. Temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017) separately calibrates the readout probabilities.

Appendix X Serving efficiency measurement details

Table 4 compares Gemma-4-31B serving efficiency on a validation/transfer workload. The tuned readout uses a merged DDS + SPRD-C checkpoint trained with Gemma’s own reasoning labels (G31X_ldm_gself). Both timed models use BF16 vLLM serving on two H100 80GB GPUs each, with prefix caching disabled. On 32 sequential validation/transfer inputs repeated twice, tuned readout has a median response latency of 40.6 ms, versus 7.38 s for reasoning rollout. On 128 inputs at concurrency 32, also repeated twice, throughput is 44.2 and 0.787 requests/s, respectively. Readout therefore reduces median latency by 182×\times and increases throughput by 56.2×\times relative to reasoning rollout. The timer covers host-local HTTP requests through response parsing, excluding prompt preparation, model loading and compilation. The serving API returns one option token to expose candidate scores, with no subsequent autoregressive decode step, while reasoning averages 1,027 output tokens in the concurrent workload. Allocated GPU-hours per million requests are extrapolated as two GPUs times measured job duration divided by completed requests, scaled to one million; they exclude loading, compilation and training. Speedups in Table 4 are computed from the displayed median latencies. These measurements do not measure confidence-router latency. The serving backend also applies Gemma’s logit softcapping, unlike the original raw-logit scorer, so its probabilities require separate calibration before routing.
